title: What is cultural heritage? Meaning, types and Indian examples
seo_title: What is Cultural Heritage? Meaning, Types and Examples
meta_description: What is cultural heritage? Its meaning, tangible and intangible types, Indian examples and who protects it, with short notes for students and teachers.
summary: Cultural heritage is what a community inherits from earlier generations and chooses to keep and pass on: buildings, sites, objects, manuscripts and landscapes shaped by people, along with living practices such as languages, music, dance, crafts, festivals and knowledge. In India it ranges from Harappan cities to Vedic chanting and handloom weaving.

sections.h2: Cultural heritage meaning in simple words
paras: Heritage is an inheritance. Cultural heritage is the part of that inheritance made by people rather than by nature: a temple, a coin hoard, a recipe, a script, a way of tying a turban, a folk song sung at harvest. It becomes heritage when a group recognises it as theirs, values it and wants it to survive.

That act of choosing matters. Not every old thing is heritage, and some heritage is not old at all. A twentieth century railway station or a modernist capital can be heritage because people now see it as part of who they are. The word therefore covers both the material evidence of the past and the meanings people attach to it today.

UNESCO's World Heritage Convention of 1972 gave the idea an international legal form, and its 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage extended it to living traditions. India has ratified both.
Heritage professionals usually sort cultural heritage into a few broad groups. The categories overlap, and a single place often holds all of them at once.

sections.h2: Tangible and intangible heritage: how they fit together
paras: Tangible heritage is what you can touch: stone, brick, metal, cloth, paper. Intangible heritage is what people know and do. The two depend on each other. A temple is a building, but the rituals, music, craft guilds and festival calendar that keep it alive are intangible. A Banarasi sari is an object, but the weaving skill is a living practice that disappears if no young weaver learns it.

Our guide on [what intangible cultural heritage means](what-is-intangible-cultural-heritage.html) explains the UNESCO list and India's entries on it. For buildings, the best way to understand the tangible side is to stand in front of one with someone who can read it, as on a walk around [Humayun's Tomb](humayuns-tomb.html) or the [Qutb complex](the-qutb-complex.html).

sections.h2: Examples of cultural heritage in India
paras: India's cultural heritage is unusually deep in time and wide in variety. A short list for students might include:
list: Archaeological sites: Harappan cities such as Dholavira and Rakhigarhi, Buddhist monasteries at Nalanda, painted rock shelters at Bhimbetka.
Monuments: rock-cut caves at Ajanta and Ellora, temples at Khajuraho and Thanjavur, Mughal tombs and forts in Delhi and Agra.
Historic cities: Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad), Ahmedabad, Jaipur and Varanasi.
Scripts and texts: Brahmi inscriptions, Sanskrit, Prakrit and Tamil literature, manuscript collections in temples and monasteries.
Performing arts: classical dance forms such as Bharatanatyam and Kathak, and folk forms such as Bihu and Ghoomar.
Crafts: handloom silks, block printing, metalwork, pottery and painted scrolls.
Knowledge systems: traditional water management, astronomy, medicine and agricultural practice.

paras: Heritage is evidence. Archaeologists and historians use buildings, objects and inscriptions to reconstruct how people lived, traded, worshipped and governed. Lose the evidence and the history becomes guesswork.

Heritage is also identity. People use it to explain where they come from and how they relate to neighbours. That makes it powerful and sometimes contested: different groups may read the same monument in different ways. A good heritage education teaches people to look at the evidence first and to hear more than one community's account.

Finally, heritage supports livelihoods. Craftspeople, guides, conservators, museum staff and performers all depend on it, which is why [heritage tourism in India](heritage-tourism-in-india.html) and conservation policy are tied together.

sections.h2: Who protects cultural heritage in India?
paras: The Archaeological Survey of India protects monuments of national importance under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. State archaeology departments protect sites of state importance. INTACH, a national non-governmental body, lists and documents unprotected buildings and runs conservation projects. Museums care for movable objects, and the Sangeet Natak Akademi and other bodies support performing arts.

Most heritage, however, is looked after by ordinary people: families who keep a haveli standing, priests and caretakers, weavers, village councils and neighbourhood groups. Our explainer on [heritage conservation in India](heritage-conservation-in-india.html) covers the law and the institutions in more detail.
If you are preparing notes for school, college or a competitive exam, keep these points in mind.
list: Definition: the legacy of physical artefacts and intangible attributes inherited from past generations, kept in the present and passed on.
Two main kinds: tangible (movable and immovable) and intangible.
Key international texts: UNESCO World Heritage Convention (1972) and the Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage (2003).
India has 45 World Heritage Sites as of October 2026, most of them cultural.
Key Indian law: AMASR Act 1958, amended in 2010.
Heritage is selected and valued by people, so it changes over time.

faq.q: What is cultural heritage in one line?
faq.a: Cultural heritage is everything people have made, practised and known that a community inherits from earlier generations and chooses to keep and hand on, from monuments and objects to languages, songs, crafts and festivals.

faq.q: What are the two main types of cultural heritage?
faq.a: Tangible heritage, which includes monuments, sites and movable objects such as sculptures, coins and manuscripts, and intangible heritage, which covers living practices such as performing arts, rituals, festivals, oral traditions and craft skills. Many places combine both.

faq.q: What is the difference between natural and cultural heritage?
faq.a: Natural heritage is made by nature: forests, mountains, rivers and wildlife habitats such as Kaziranga or the Western Ghats. Cultural heritage is made or shaped by people. A mixed site, like Khangchendzonga in Sikkim, is valued for both its nature and its cultural meaning.

faq.q: Give five examples of cultural heritage of India.
faq.a: The Taj Mahal, the Ajanta caves, the Harappan city of Dholavira, the Sanskrit theatre tradition of Kutiyattam, and the Kumbh Mela. The first three are tangible World Heritage Sites; the last two are on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

faq.q: Is a modern building ever cultural heritage?
faq.a: Yes. Heritage is about value, not only age. Le Corbusier's Capitol Complex in Chandigarh and the Art Deco buildings of Mumbai are recent but are World Heritage Sites because people recognise them as significant to India's story.
